qs.q: What is the gold diagnostic tool for confirming Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) in patients with systemic sclerosis?
qs.e: Right-sided heart catheterization is the gold diagnostic tool to confirm pulmonary arterial hypertension, whereas echocardiography is used as the initial investigation. PFTs may show an isolated low DLCO, but catheterization is definitive.

qs.q: Which autoantibody is noted to be extremely specific for CREST syndrome and is associated with the limited subset of systemic sclerosis, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and digital ulcers?
qs.e: Anti-centromere antibodies are extremely specific for CREST syndrome and are linked to the limited subset of systemic sclerosis and pulmonary arterial hypertension. In contrast, Scl-70 is associated with the diffuse subset and ILD.

qs.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic tool for Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension in systemic sclerosis?
qs.e: The note identifies right-sided heart catheterization as the gold diagnostic tool for PAH. Echocardiography is the first investigation to order but is not the gold standard.

ai.clinicalScope: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in adult patients in low‑resource East African hospitals, focusing on common tropical causes and limited investigations
ai.title: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: PAH is a progressive vasculopathy of the pulmonary arteries causing right‑ventricular failure. In low‑resource settings, HIV, schistosomiasis, and congenital heart disease are frequent drivers. Early recognition and risk‑adapted therapy improve survival.

sections.p: PAH is defined by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥25 mmHg at rest, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≤15 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance >3 WU on right‑heart catheterisation. In many centres, a transthoracic echo with a systolic PAP >35 mmHg plus clinical suspicion is used as a pragmatic screen.

t.b: Estimate systolic PAP and assess RV size/function – a PAP >35 mmHg suggests PAH
Confirm haemodynamics and calculate PVR – definitive diagnosis

sections.p: The REVEAL 2.0 score and WHO functional class guide prognosis and therapy. In resource‑limited settings, WHO class and echo findings are often used to stratify risk.

t.b: Assesses symptom burden – FC III/IV indicates high risk

sections.p: In East Africa, the top causes are HIV infection, schistosomiasis, and untreated congenital heart disease. Other tropical infections and rheumatic heart disease can also contribute.

t.b: High VL correlates with PAH risk – consider antiretroviral optimisation
Positive IgG suggests chronic infection – treat with praziquantel

sections.p: Patients often report progressive exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and peripheral oedema. Early signs include a loud P2, right‑sided heart failure, and syncope.

t.b: Look for RV heave, displaced apex, and raised JVP – indicates RV strain

sections.p: A pragmatic workup uses history, exam, echo, basic labs, and targeted imaging. Advanced tests may be unavailable; alternatives are outlined.
b: Echo for PAP and RV assessment
Basic labs: CBC, LFTs, HIV RNA, Schistosoma serology

t.b: Rule out interstitial lung disease or large pulmonary emboli – normal in isolated PAH
Exclude COPD/ILD – normal FEV1/FVC suggests PAH
Exclude acute pulmonary embolism – normal value reduces suspicion of CTEPH

sections.p: Acute right‑ventricular failure, haemoptysis, and sudden death are life‑threatening. Watch for signs of RV decompensation and bleeding.

t.b: May indicate ruptured pulmonary artery aneurysm – urgent imaging and airway protection

sections.p: Treat underlying causes first, then initiate PAH‑specific therapy based on risk. In low‑resource settings, generic endothelin receptor antagonists and PDE‑5 inhibitors are preferred when available.
b: Correction of congenital shunts if feasible

t.b: Oral endothelin receptor antagonist – improves exercise capacity
Oral PDE‑5 inhibitor – improves haemodynamics and symptoms

sections.p: Monitor clinical status, echo, and biomarkers every 3–6 months in high‑risk patients. Preventive measures include HIV counselling, schistosomiasis control, and early CHD repair.

t.b: Assess PAP and RV size – changes guide therapy adjustment

sections.p: Pulmonary hypertension due to left‑heart disease (Group 2) and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) can mimic PAH but have different treatments.
b: Left‑heart disease – treat LV failure first

t.b: Elevated in left‑heart disease – distinguishes from PAH

sections.p: A normal D‑dimer does not exclude CTEPH; a normal chest X‑ray may miss small emboli. Spirometry may be normal in early PAH.

t.b: Normal value does not rule out CTEPH – proceed to V/Q scan if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe dyspnoea or chest pain

faq.q: Why is HIV a risk factor for PAH?
faq.a: HIV causes chronic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, promoting pulmonary vascular remodeling.
No; treatment slows progression and improves quality of life, but the underlying vasculopathy is irreversible.

faq.q: What is the first drug to start in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: An oral endothelin receptor antagonist like bosentan, if available, or a PDE‑5 inhibitor such as tadalafil.

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with progressive dyspnoea. What is the next best investigation? — Echo to estimate PAP and assess RV function; if high, proceed to right‑heart cath.

A patient with PAH develops sudden haemoptysis. What is the most likely complication and immediate management? — Pulmonary artery aneurysm rupture; secure airway, give oxygen, and arrange urgent CT angiography.
You suspect PAH in a patient with a normal chest X‑ray and normal spirometry. What is the most appropriate next step? — Right‑heart catheterisation to confirm haemodynamics.
A patient with WHO FC III PAH is stable on bosentan. Which drug should you add if symptoms persist? — A PDE‑5 inhibitor such as tadalafil to improve exercise capacity.
In a setting without a cath lab, how would you diagnose PAH? — Use echo criteria (PAP >35 mmHg) plus clinical assessment and risk stratification.
A patient with PAH is on bosentan but develops liver enzyme elevation. What is the next step? — Discontinue bosentan, monitor LFTs, and consider switching to a PDE‑5 inhibitor.
What is the main difference between PAH and CTEPH on imaging? — CTEPH shows organised thrombus in pulmonary arteries on CT or V/Q scan; PAH shows normal pulmonary arteries but elevated pressures.
Why is a normal D‑dimer not sufficient to rule out CTEPH? — D‑dimer can be normal in chronic thromboembolic disease; a V/Q scan is required for diagnosis.
